new_statements.rule_in_words: Kutu, an East Ruvu language adjacent to Swahili, is reported to have lost lexical/grammatical tone and to share the areal Swahili-type pattern of stress on the penultimate syllable of the word. This is a comparative, group-level statement (Kutu is named explicitly only for tone loss); no first-hand description of Kutu prosody exists.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the authors flag the Swahili origin of the areal penult stress as a guess ('the evidence is not conclusive').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level penultimate stress as an areal feature; no discussion of phrase vs word domain or citation forms for Kutu. The closest first-hand modern description is of the sister language Kami (Petzell & Aunio 2019: 'regular penultimate stress and no tonal contrast'), and Meinhof 1907 gives penult dynamic accent for Zaramo; both are different languages of the same East Ruvu cluster.
new_statements.identity_note: No source describes Kutu (kutu1263) prosody first-hand. The only explicit prosodic mention of Kutu is Philippson's comparative remark in Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993 (tone loss, p.524); the penultimate-stress remark (p.558) is about 'adjacent East Ruvu languages' as a group (East Ruvu = Zaramo, Kwere, Kutu, Kami, Doe in Nurse & Philippson's classification). First-hand penult-stress statements exist only for sister languages: Kami kami1256 (Petzell & Aunio 2019) and Zaramo zara1247 (Meinhof 1907). Zahran 2023 (Petzell's student) treats Kutu-Kwere-Zalamo as a dialect continuum and states there is no linguistic work focusing on Kutu.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule (stress on syllable 2 of 2, 2 of 3, 3 of 4 = penultimate) and the existing p.558 statement;248 subject ('East Ruvu languages have lost all prosodic distinctiveness, as has Swahili', previously inferred, now verbatim in the window) and the p.524 sentence naming Kutu among the languages into which the loss of tonal distinctiveness spread. The evidence remains second-hand and group-level (East Ruvu), not a description of Kutu.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kutu is treated only as a member of the East Ruvu group: the East Ruvu languages (Kutu among them, named explicitly on p.524) have lost tonal/prosodic distinctiveness and, like Swahili, have penultimate stress, which the authors take to be an areal feature that spread from Swahili into adjacent East Ruvu. Page-unlocated windows from the same conclusions add the authors' framing: 'tone' was replaced by 'accent' at an early point in all NEC languages except Pare (Ruvu?) (Chap. 2, sec. 16); 'to talk of the replacement of tone by stress is inaccurate: loss of tone/pitch and/or stress taking over the functions of tone/pitch is more appropriate'; and 'loss of pitch distinctions originated somewhere in Swahili, and diffused along the Swahili spectrum and into East Ruvu.' No Kutu-specific stress data, examples or rule are given; there is no Kutu phonology in the book (search-inside 'Kutu' = 9 hits, all consonant reflexes, lexicon, classification lists, one TA form).
new_statements.exceptions: none for Kutu. The only exceptions named are other languages: Mwiini (no penultimate stress) and Mwani (movable pitch accent, retaining vestiges of pitch); West Ruvu (Kagulu, Lugulu, probably Sagala) has not lost prosodic distinctiveness.
new_statements.identity_note: Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993 name no Kutu dialect; Kutu (G37) appears only as one of the East Ruvu languages (East Ruvu = Zaramo, Doe, Kutu, Kami, Kwere/Nhwele in their classification; West Ruvu = Kagulu, Lugulu, Sagala per the p.248 window). The penultimate-stress statement is made for 'adjacent East Ruvu languages' as a group and for Kutu explicitly only in the tone-loss list on p.524.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level, second-hand statement: the East Ruvu languages (of which Kutu is one, named on p. 524) have lost tonal/prosodic distinctiveness and share the areal penultimate stress of Swahili; i.e. non-contrastive word stress on the penultimate syllable. new_statements.identity_note: Kutu = Kikutu/Khutu, ISO kdc, Guthrie G37c, East Ruvu (with Kwere, Zalamo, Doe, Kami), Morogoro Region, Tanzania. Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993 treat Kutu only as an 'adjacent language' to the Sabaki group; every prosodic statement touching it is at the East Ruvu group level, not a description of a Kutu variety.
